newsitem.title: UK: Celltech says FDA "encouraging" on leukaemia.
newsitem.headline: Celltech says FDA "encouraging" on leukaemia.

text.p: Celltech Group Plc said on Tuesday that talks held with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) about its acute leukaemia drug CMA 676 had been "encouraging."
In an interview with Reuters, chief executive Peter Fellner said Celltech's partner on the ground-breaking drug, American Home Products Corp, "has had a meeting with the FDA which was encouraging."
He said that American Home was now planning to launch a Phase II/III trial of the drug, which could potentially replace chemotherapy, in March or April.
He said the study would involve 55 patients in 10 centres who had already had one dose of chemotherapy but then relapsed.
The drug consists of a cell-killing drug, Calicheamicin, developed by American Home, and a Celltech-developed antibody.

The antibody accurately targets the cancer cells with the cell-killing drug. Phase I/II trials showed that more than half of 36 patients who had failed previous treatments responded to the drug, while two showed complete remission.
Fellner said the product had only mild side effects, giving it a major edge over chemotherapy.
"We would like it to be better, more effective, than chemotherapy.. but it doesn't have to be. It only has to be as good, because the safety profile is so much better," he said.
A European study invlolving 50 patients who are unsuitable for chemotherapy is also planned.
"If American Home find... that it has similar efficacy to chemotherapy then we are in very good shape," Fellner said.

Trials could be completed in the first half of 1998, with registration possible in the second half of the year, Fellner said. He said the product would sell for at least $10,000 per course of treatment. The British company would receive an undisclosed royalty from American Home on worldwide sales.
The same American Home drug has been linked to another Celltech "magic bullet" which targets ovarian cancer and small cell lung cancer, Fellner said.
A phase I/II study in ovarian cancer is currently about half way through, with results likely in the second half of this year.
Fellner told Reuters that clinical trials of the drug in non-small cell lung cancer -- which accounts for around 70 percent of all lung cancers -- would start at the end of March.
